title: Pharmacoresistance may be an evolved form of network adaptation

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Pharmacoresistance may be an evolved form of network adaptation

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Because random ODE networks rarely show habituation in more than 30% of stimulus–response pairs while biological pathway models differ from that distribution, pharmacoresistance (habituation) may be a form of network adaptation more prevalent in networks shaped by evolutionary pressure, not due to network properties alone.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: Learning in Transcriptional Network Models: Computational Discovery of Pathway-Level Memory and Effective Interventions

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Biswas S 2022, Learning in Transcriptional Network Models: Computational Discovery of Pathway-Level Memory and Effective Interventions › 2. Results › 2.7. Making and Breaking Pharmacoresistance

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: This would hint that pharmacoresistance may be a form of network adaptation, which would indeed be more prevalent in a biological network shaped by evolutionary pressure.

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Biswas S, Clawson W, Levin M, “Learning in Transcriptional Network Models: Computational Discovery of Pathway-Level Memory and Effective Interventions”, International journal of molecular sciences (2022), doi:10.3390/ijms24010285; section “2. Results › 2.7. Making and Breaking Pharmacoresistance”. Scope: BioModels pathway models versus 500 random gene-circuit models

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on levin-2022-grn-learning-15: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.54

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Existing models can resolve the reported distributional difference. They cannot cleanly identify evolutionary adaptation as its cause because the null ensemble is not an exchangeable unevolved control.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Confirm the biological-versus-random habituation distribution, then compare evolved and null ensembles under multiple kinetic and topology-matching schemes. An evolutionary explanation would require enrichment robust to null choices plus independent evidence of selection.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Repository selection and model complexity confound the comparison.

Biological and synthetic random models differ in more than evolutionary history.

fields.value:

discriminating power: 0.32
analysis feasibility: 0.64
data existence: 0.78
data adequacy: 0.38

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The biological-versus-random habituation contrast can be recomputed. The claim that pharmacoresistance is an adaptation produced by evolutionary pressure does not follow from that contrast, because model-building bias and a mismatched equation class are equally compatible with the same numbers. Only a weak proxy is testable now.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compare the distribution of habituating pair fractions in the biological models with the 500 random circuits, using a 30 percent pair-fraction cutoff. A biological distribution shifted above that random ceiling would reproduce the contrast; overlap would remove the stated hint. Neither result identifies evolutionary pressure as the cause.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Curated published models are enriched for interesting dynamics independently of selection.

The random circuits are not evolutionarily naive versions of the same pathways.
